extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, literary practitioners, and general readers interested in the vocation and practice of writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and moral guidance for authorship: routines, research and revision practices, motives for writing, and views on copyright and the aims of literature. A 19th-century essay advising aspiring writers how to work, why to write, and what to value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and drafting routine
rubrics_metrics.description: “I oftener wrote out my first draft, merely indicating extracts where such were to be quoted ... but I sometimes dictated to my secretary, who took short-hand notes ... My first chapter was thus composed at one sitting ... usually, two days, or even three, were given to the composition of each of the longer chapters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and digest material before composing; choose a drafting method that suits you (written first draft or dictation to a secretary); allocate focused time per chapter (one to several days); indicate long quotations for later insertion. Practical notes include delegating transcription and preparing material in advance to speed composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect concentrated working time
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our rule was to lock the door on resuming composition, and decline all solicitations to open it till the day's allotted task had been finished ... I would allow the location of my 'den' to be known to but one person ... and I would have that door open to no one beside but my secretary and myself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish disciplined boundaries: remove interruptions, limit who may intrude, and reserve dedicated space/time for writing. Treat focused solitude as an essential enabler of productive composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and proof-correction workflow
rubrics_metrics.description: “A chapter having been fairly written out or transcribed ... I carefully revised and sent it to the stereotyper, who sent me his second and third proofs, which were successively corrected before the pages were ready to be cast.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an iterative proofreading cycle: revise carefully before sending to production, review successive proofs (second, third, etc.), and correct at each stage. Be prepared for post-publication corrections when new evidence emerges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to recast chapters when new material arises
rubrics_metrics.description: “Sometimes, the discovery of new material compelled the revision and recast of a chapter which had been passed as complete.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat finished chapters as potentially provisional: integrate newly discovered sources or facts even if it requires substantial rewriting. Expect and accept recasting as part of rigorous historical/literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and verification of authorities/primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: “I wished to study it in the proceedings and debates ... of these I found but a single file preserved ... Of the score or so of speeches made by Jefferson Davis ... I found but two condensed reports; and one of these, I apprehend, was apocryphal ... In many cases, I found officers reported killed in battles whom I afterward found fighting in subsequent battles.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on primary sources when possible, but cross-check and corroborate because contemporary reports can be incomplete, contradictory, or apocryphal. Seek multiple independent attestations for key facts; remain skeptical of single uncorroborated reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct factual errors when credible evidence appears
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some of the errors into which I was thus led by my authorities were not corrected till after my work was printed; when the gentlemen thus conclusively disposed of began to write me, insisting that ... they had decided not to give up the ghost ... Their testimony was so direct and pointed that I was constrained to believe it, and to correct page after page accordingly.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to reliable, direct testimony or evidence by correcting the public record; acknowledge and fix mistakes even after publication. Accept that despite care, some errors will remain and should be remedied when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: greater particularity increases usefulness but raises error risk
rubrics_metrics.description: “... as I have stated many more particulars than my rivals in the same field have usually done, it is probable that my work originally embodied more errors of fact or incident than almost any other.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including more particulars and particulars of incident makes a work more valuable to readers and historians but increases exposure to factual mistakes; authors must weigh comprehensiveness against the risk of errors and be ready to correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from intrinsic love of the work (proper motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of the legions who aspire to Write ... only a very small proportion do so from any hearty, intrinsic, essential love of the work, while the great multitude seek primarily and mainly their own glory or aggrandizement.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to write out of genuine desire to teach, enlighten, or create, not chiefly for money, fame, or ease. The author’s motive affects the quality and sincerity of the work; self-interested motives are presented as anti-patterns that produce inferior literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: write to teach, dispel ignorance, and benefit humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The chief business of life is Education ... Happy he ... who comes divinely qualified for a Teacher, — fitted by nature and training to wrestle with giant Ignorance ... To govern men ... is a small achievement; the true king ... is he who sways the mighty realm of Thought.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceive of authorship as an educational, moral vocation: aim to enlighten, dispel prejudice, and contribute enduring ideas. Value influence over power; seek to address universal human concerns rather than transient local tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement to publish despite market saturation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Heed not the croaker's warning that the world overflows with books and authors ... if you have something to say, and do really say it, never doubt that it will find or make its way to the eyes and hearts of those fitted to appreciate and enjoy it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be deterred by the abundance of books; quality and sincerity will find an audience. The market’s apparent saturation is not a valid reason to withhold a meaningful work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to provincial prejudices for short-term gain
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Law of Copyright ... is doubly wrong in virtually saying to the author, 'Cater to the prejudices, the follies, the passions of the hour; for the approval of future generations ... will give no bread to your famishing offspring!'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist incentives (legal or commercial) that push authors to write to immediate popular tastes at the expense of enduring merit. Speak to broader humanity rather than tailoring work solely to local/temporal prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: High ambition: seek lasting intellectual influence rather than temporal power
rubrics_metrics.description: “The true king ... is he who sways the mighty realm of Thought ... compare Plato, and Virgil, and Tacitus ... with Alexander or Augustus.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspire to be remembered for contributions to ideas and letters; prioritize work that will outlast ephemeral political or material achievements. The metric of greatness is enduring cultural/intellectual impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: View of authorship as mixed labor (mental + physical) with moral/property implications
rubrics_metrics.description: “A poem, as given by the author to the press, is the joint production of intellect and muscles ... The difference is one of proportion only ... The Law of Copyright is pernicious in all its restrictions on the natural right of property ... The law plunders the author while pretending to protect him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the material and creative aspects of producing books; defend the moral claim that authorship is a form of property deserving fair legal protection. Critique existing copyright practices that limit authors' rights by territory or time and argue for fair compensation if rights are later confiscated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on convictions and accept personal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: “The public has learned that I act upon my convictions without fear of personal consequences; hence, any future paroxysm of popular rage against me is likely to be less violent ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to stand by principled positions in writing even if unpopular; moral courage can mitigate future backlash and is presented as an ethical duty of the author.
